schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'there fell upon him spirit of God' and confesses the prophet unknown — Oded shares the radical letters of Iddo, but identity is beyond decision.
Gill, following Hillerus and the Jews, would identify Azariah with Iddo, the prophet once sent to reprove Jeroboam; the Targum reads 'the spirit of prophecy.'
Henry reads the prophet as heaven's mercy to an idolatrous people — sent to quicken a victorious army to duty, not to compliment it.
Clarke: nothing is known of the prophet but this chapter; Wesley: the Spirit came both to instruct him what to say and to enable him to say it plainly and boldly.

debates.question: Is the prophet Azariah the same as Iddo?

sides.position: the same as Iddo, the prophet who reproved Jeroboam
an otherwise unknown prophet; the identification is beyond decision

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the echo of Abijah's speech (2 Chron 13:4), renders 'Jehovah was with you in the battle because ye were with him,' and calls the seek/forsake clause a favourite formula of the chronicler.
Clarke reads the double clause as God's settled purpose and a flat denial of unconditional perseverance, quoting the Targum's paraphrase on the Word of the LORD as helper.
Henry takes the maxim as both comfort and caution — God's favour is a tenancy hanging on perseverance, and the diligent seeker is never dismissed in vain (Heb. 11:6).
Gill sets the scene: the prophet went out from Jerusalem to meet Asa returning to it.

themes: with you while you are with him

schools.summary: Keil reads a general present, tasted in the Judges but deepened in the future exile (Hosea 3:4); Ellicott calls it an illustration of the general truth, adducing the declines of Judges 2:11ff. and grounding 'teaching priest' in Lev 10:11 and Mal 2:7.
Clarke settles for the recent past under Rehoboam and Abijah, changed by Asa; Wesley casts it further back to the whole nation's lapses in the days of the Judges.
Gill leaves the period unexpressed, canvassing the Targum's ten-tribes reading and the alternative fulfilment in the Babylonish captivity.

debates.question: What time does 'many days without the true God' describe?

sides.position: the past anarchy of the days of the Judges and former apostasies
the recent state of the ten tribes / the reigns of Rehoboam and Abijah, changed under Asa
a future desolation, fulfilled under the idolatrous kings and in the exile

outliers.note: Lays all three readings side by side — the Judges, the ten tribes under Asa, and a future desolation — without deciding, content that all were written for our admonition.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'he returned in his straits unto Jehovah,' ties it to the promise of Deut 4:30, and documents the cycle of oppression and deliverance from Judges 3:9ff. and Ps 106:44.
Gill reads the full movement of repentance — oppressed Israel cried, repented, turned from their sins, and were heard.
Henry: when trouble drove them to God they found it not in vain to seek him — the record set down to invite even backsliders home.
Ellicott anchors 'those times' to the 'many days' of v.3, traces the unsafe highways to Judges 5:6, and renders 'great vexations' as 'confusions' — the covenant curse of Deut 28:20.
Wesley pictures men unable to travel safely, as in the days of Shamgar (Judges 5:6); Clarke asks whether Christ alludes to this verse in Matt 24:6-7.
Gill reads the collapse of ordinary life — highways infested with thieves, no safety for the traveller.
Henry: the forsaken nation harassed with destroying wars foreign and domestic — provoking God with all iniquity, vexed with all adversity.

themes: no peace going out or coming in
provoked with iniquity, vexed with adversity

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'crushed, nation by nation,' taking goy as a clan and pointing to the feuds of Judges 12 and 20 and the strife of Isaiah 19:2; Keil expounds the verb as the confusion God brings to destroy his enemies (Exod 14:24), tasted in the Judges and deepened in the exile (Hosea 3:4).
Gill takes 'nation of nation' of the tribes — Ephraim by Gilead, Benjamin by the rest, Shechem by Abimelech.
Wesley: one part of Israel destroyed the other by civil wars, the tribes themselves called nations.
Henry: they provoked God with all iniquity, and he vexed them with all adversity.

themes: confusion from the hand of God

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the verse the moral of the address — 'But ye, be ye strong,' hands that must not 'droop' (Zeph 3:16), 'a reward for your work' (Jer 31:16), the work being the rooting out of idolatry.
Wesley: go on resolutely to maintain God's worship and root out idolatry — the only method of escaping the calamities the fathers felt.
Gill: be hearty and vigorous, not languid, in the reformation Asa had begun.
Henry: God's work needs resolution, and its certain reward should quicken us — for the work is its own reward.

themes: be strong, let not your hands droop

schools.summary: Ellicott finds 'the prophecy Oded the prophet' suspicious — a gloss or lacuna — and glosses 'took courage' (strengthened himself, cf. v.7), 'abominable idols' (shiqqutsim), and mount Ephraim (Abijah's conquests, 2 Chron 13:19); Keil records the conjecture that 'son of Azariah' dropped out.
Gill takes Oded for Azariah himself, noting the Vulgate, Syriac, and Alexandrian LXX read 'Azariah the son of Oded.'
Wesley: 'of Oded' means Azariah under his father's name; Clarke reads 'renewed the altar' as re-dedicated or enlarged for more sacrifices.
Henry: the message gave the king more courage than his victory had, to destroy all idols (1 Pet 4:3) and repair an altar already worn (Heb 8:13).

debates.question: Is 'Oded the prophet' (v.8) the same as Azariah son of Oded (v.1), or a textual fault?

sides.position: Oded is Azariah himself, named by his father's name
the phrase is a suspicious gloss or lacuna in the text

debates.question: What was the 'renewing' of the altar?

sides.position: a re-dedication or enlargement for more sacrifices
a reconsecration of an altar defiled by illegal worship (LXX/Vulg 'dedicated'), or merely a repair

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the migration among the accessions under Rehoboam (2 Chron 11:16) and Hezekiah (2 Chron 30:11) and weighs the puzzle of Simeon (Gen 49:7); Keil fixes the festival in Asa's fifteenth year, soon after the Cushite war.
Clarke reads their motive: piety drew them from Jeroboam's idolatrous government to the worship of the true God, the blessing being promised to David's house.
Gill glosses the strangers as proselytes of the gate.
Henry: they came because they saw God was with Asa — good to keep company with those who have God with them (Zech 8:23).

themes: because the LORD was with him

schools.summary: Keil sets the feast soon after the Cushite war (the offering drawn from Zerah's spoil, 2 Chron 14:14) and weighs the chronology of Asa's eleventh and fifteenth years.
Clarke fixes the third month as the time of Pentecost.
Gill notes they came together by the order of Asa.
Henry hears in 'they gathered themselves' (v.10) the readiness of a willing people, matching Asa's command with their own act, probably at Pentecost.

Ellicott dates the offering to the third month, Sivan, from the spoil of Zerah and the cities round Gerar (2 Chron 14:13-15); Keil notes 'they brought of the spoil' defines the sacrifice and shows the feast followed hard on the victory.
Gill identifies the spoil from the Ethiopian camp and the Philistine cities, the Targum setting it on the feast of weeks.
Clarke traces the victims to the plunder taken from Zerah and his auxiliaries (2 Chron 14:14-15).
Henry weighs the offering against Solomon's greater one (2 Chron 7:5), reads it as thanksgiving and supplication, and lifts it to the gospel's spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise.
Ellicott: the phrase means they bound themselves by oath (cf. Jer 34:10; Neh 10:29), 'with all their heart' echoing Deut 4:29; Keil reads it as a renewal of the covenant already theirs.
Clarke sets out the covenant in two articles — to seek the true God, and to punish idolatry with death — confirmed by oath, so no toleration was given to idolatry.
Gill, with Piscator, notes they passed between the pieces of a calf cut asunder to ratify the covenant (cf. Jer 34:18).
Henry: penitents rightly renew their covenants — increasing their sense of obligation, arming against temptation, and strengthening one another's hands to seek God with all the heart.
Ellicott calls it part of the solemn oath, a sanction from Deut 13:6ff. and 17:2-6; Keil reads it as the proof of a sincere return — punishing defection by death per Deut 17:2-6.
Gill: it touched the obstinate idolater serving other gods, already deserving death by the law.
Henry: no law of their own making but the execution of the divine precept — yet questions whether the gospel sanctions such compulsion, for our weapons are not carnal.

Ellicott: the acclamations and blasts of trumpet and clarion enhanced the oath's solemnity (cf. 1 Chron 15:28; 2 Chron 23:13); Keil gathers it in one word — sworn aloud with joyful shouting and horns, the sign of inward gladness.
Gill reads the loud voice as holy boldness — unashamed, witnessed, without equivocation.
Henry: they swore not with a debtor's reluctance but with a bridegroom's gladness, aloud to animate one another.

Ellicott renders 'with perfect willingness' and reads 'he was found of them' as the exact fulfilment of the promise of v.2, the 'rest round about' like that of 2 Chron 14:6-7; Keil reads the sequence as cause and effect — whole-hearted seeking answered by rest.
Gill qualifies honestly: the greater part rejoiced, though some might be dissemblers.
Wesley: the times of renewing covenant should be times of rejoicing — it is honour and happiness to be in bonds with God.
Henry: God was found of them and gave them rest — national piety procures national blessings.

Ellicott identifies Maachah as Asa's grandmother and rejects the two-Maachahs theory; glosses 'queen' (gebirah, cf. Athaliah 2 Chron 22:2), 'idol' (miphletseth, a horror, cf. 1 Kings 15:13), 'grove' (for Asherah), and 'crushed' (as Moses, Exod 32:20; Josiah, 2 Kings 23:15). Keil notes the deposition is paralleled in 1 Kings 15:13.
Gill notes 'mother' means grandmother.
Henry praises the courage that would not connive at idolatry in the nearest kin (cf. Deut 33:9) — Asa deposed and probably banished the queen-mother, sparing her life as she signed the covenant.
Clarke reports the Jewish gloss that Maachah repented and was renamed Michaiah, daughter of Uriel, without endorsing it.

debates.question: Were the mother of Abijah and the 'mother' of Asa the same Maachah?

sides.position: the same woman, grandmother of Asa, deposed for her idolatry

holders: others (as reported and rejected by Ellicott)

outliers.note: Passes on the Jewish legend that Maachah repented and had her name changed to Michaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, so her former name might not reproach her.

schools.summary: Ellicott: 2 Chron 14:3 records what Asa resolved and attempted, 15:17 his lack of success against the people's attachment (cf. the pair 17:6 / 20:33); 'out of Israel' means the south, and the 'perfect heart' means fidelity to the temple worship (1 Chron 28:9).
Clarke: the idolatry was totally suppressed, but some places, buildings, or altars were permitted to remain.
Henry distinguishes the false high places removed from the irregular ones connived at, and finds the lesson that sincerity is something less than sinless perfection.

debates.question: How is 'the high places were not taken away' reconciled with their removal in 2 Chron 14?

sides.position: 14:3 records what Asa resolved and attempted; 15:17 his want of success against the people's attachment
the idolatry was suppressed but some buildings/altars, or the high places used for the true God, were left standing

schools.summary: Ellicott notes the verse is identical with 1 Kings 15:15 (God for Jehovah); the dedicated things were from Abijah's spoils (2 Chron 13:16-19) and Asa's Cushite booty (2 Chron 14:13-15) — the Kings verse confirming the chronicler's account of victories he alone records.
Clarke: by custom a part of the spoils was dedicated; Abijah's plunder from Jeroboam (2 Chron 13:15-19) was only now brought in; 'vessels' is kelim — instruments, utensils, ornaments.
Henry reads it as honesty toward God — rendering him his own without delay, for will a man rob God (Mal 3:8)?

Ellicott and Keil harmonize the 'no war' with Kings by distinguishing open conflict from the latent, inherited hostility of the two kingdoms; Ellicott relays Thenius' conjecture that the date is a copyist's inflation of an original fifth/sixth year.
Gill: no war with any foreign enemy after the Ethiopian war, though continual bickerings with Baasha.
Clarke offers Usher's reckoning from the division of the kingdom (Asa's 15th year) or a reading of 'twenty-fifth,' confessing the difficulty of all such chronologies.
Henry reads the mercy — a long reprieve of peace, no open general war though frontier skirmishes remained.

debates.question: How is the problematic 'five and thirtieth year' to be explained?

sides.position: count the years from the division of the kingdom (Usher), giving Asa's fifteenth year
a textual corruption; the original figures were the fifth and sixth years

themes: no more war until the 35th year
